newsitem.title: USA: Mars rover to probe "Barnacle Bill", other rocks.
newsitem.headline: Mars rover to probe "Barnacle Bill", other rocks.

text.p: The exploration of Mars entered a new stage on Sunday with the Pathfinder's roving vehicle Sojourner preparing to set its sights on a multi-coloured rock dubbed "Barnacle Bill."

The Sojourner, a solar-powered vehicle about the size of a microwave oven, rolled out of the Pathfinder lander late on Saturday and was parked in the Martian dust for the night. In a few hours, scientists will upload a series of commands to the Sojourner to back up, pivot slightly and begin its exploration of the rocks and soil.
The Sojourner's mission, which was described as the robotic equivalent of Neil Armstrong's historic landing on the moon in 1969, is clearly the high point for the $266 million project.
"Everything is going absolutely perfectly," Project Scientist Matthew Golombek told reporters at a briefing at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory here.
"We're just more excited than you can believe. We've never got a measurement from a rock on Mars. This is a great rock."
Once the Sojourner completes its examination of the rock -- dubbed "Barnacle Bill" because it appears to be covered with little markings -- the rover will move on to a larger rock, dubbed "Yogi".
NASA officials hope the tests will tell them about Mars' intriguing past, including how the rocks were formed and whether there may ever have been life on the so-called "Red Planet".
According to some of the preliminary pictures transmitted back to Earth since the Pathfinder landed on Friday, Mars is a rust-coloured planet with a wide variety of angular and rounded rocks.

On the horizon of the landing site, scientists can see a twin-peaked area with what appears to be a white-coloured "ski slope" on one side and a series of horizontal bands on the other. Scientists believe the features were formed by a series of devastating floods that covered the region billions of years ago.
"These are all indications of water activity," said Ronald Greeley, one of the mission scientists from Arizona State University.

The Pathfinder's landing site, an ancient flood plain called Ares Vallis, was chosen because of its relatively flat terrain and abundance of rocks that were washed down into the basin during what scientists believe was a catastrophic flood.

The Sojourner "awoke" late on Saturday night after officials were able to restore communications to the solar-powered craft and issue a series of commands that allowed it to roll off the Pathfinder's ramp and park on the planet's surface.

Pictures transmitted from the surface of the planet showed the high-tech Sojourner sitting about a vehicle's length away from the lander vehicle. One image taken by the rover's binocular camera showed the ramp as it drove slowly down the 35-degree slope.
A distinct track from the six-wheeled rover was visible -- the first sign of terrestrial life since the Viking missions of the 1970's took thousands of photographs.
A camera on the lander will begin taking high-resolution photographs of the region in order to chart the solar-powered Sojourner's exploration over the next week.
Pathfinder crash-landed on Mars on Friday after a seven month journey of 309 million miles (497 million km) since being launched from Cape Canaveral.
The mission marks the beginning of an ambitious U.S. programme over the next decade to explore Mars and determine if it ever supported any life forms.
